techniques.name: Safety Envelope Testing
techniques.description: Safety envelope testing systematically evaluates AI system performance at the boundaries of its intended operational domain to identify potential failure modes before deployment. The technique involves defining the system's operational design domain (ODD), creating test scenarios that approach or exceed these boundaries, and measuring performance degradation as conditions become more challenging. By testing edge cases, environmental extremes, and boundary conditions, it reveals where the system transitions from safe to unsafe operation, enabling the establishment of clear operational limits and safety margins for deployment.

example_use_cases.description: Testing autonomous vehicle perception systems at the limits of weather conditions, lighting, and sensor coverage to establish safe operational boundaries and determine when human intervention is required.
Evaluating medical AI diagnostic systems with edge cases near decision boundaries to ensure reliable performance and identify when the system should defer to human specialists.
Assessing financial trading algorithms under extreme market conditions and volatility to prevent catastrophic losses and ensure system shutdown protocols activate appropriately.

limitations.description: Requires comprehensive domain expertise to identify relevant boundary conditions and edge cases that could affect system safety.
May be computationally expensive and time-consuming, especially for complex systems with high-dimensional operational domains.
Difficult to achieve complete coverage of all possible boundary conditions, potentially missing critical edge cases.
Results may not generalise to novel scenarios that fall outside the tested boundary conditions.
Establishing appropriate safety thresholds and performance criteria requires careful calibration based on domain-specific risk tolerance.

techniques.name: Scenario-Based Simulation Testing
techniques.description: Scenario-based simulation testing checks an automated system, most often an automated driving system, by running it through a planned set of situations in a simulator and judging each run against criteria fixed in advance. Scenarios are written at three levels of detail: a functional scenario describes a situation in words (a car cuts in ahead on a motorway), a logical scenario turns it into parameters with ranges (speeds, gaps, road friction), and a concrete scenario fixes one value for every parameter so that the run can be reproduced exactly. Functional scenarios are derived from hazard analysis and from the operational design domain (the conditions the system is designed to work in), and concrete scenarios are sampled from the logical ranges, either to cover the whole range or to seek out rare, critical combinations. Each concrete scenario is executed with the system under test in the loop, and pass or fail is decided against its expected behaviour, such as no collision, or by criticality measures such as time-to-collision, giving a record of which situations the system handles and which it does not. ISO 34502 sets out this process as a safety evaluation framework for automated driving systems.

example_use_cases.description: A developer of a motorway driving function derives cut-in, cut-out and stopped-vehicle scenarios from its hazard analysis, gives each logical scenario ranges for speeds, gaps and road friction, and runs several thousand sampled concrete scenarios in simulation for every software release, holding back any release in which a run ends in a collision the function was required to avoid.

A robotaxi operator rebuilds the fatal crashes recorded over a decade in the city where it operates as concrete simulation scenarios, and replays each one with its driving system in place of first one human driver and then the other, so that it can show regulators how the system behaves in the crash types that actually occur in its operating area.

An operator of an autonomous passenger ferry tests its collision-avoidance planner on head-on, crossing and overtaking encounters described in the international collision regulations, varying the other vessel's speed, bearing and visibility in a ship simulator, and checks in every run that the ferry keeps its required passing distance and makes the manoeuvre the regulations call for.

limitations.description: The evidence covers only the scenarios that were specified. Real operating conditions cannot be listed exhaustively, so a clean result shows that the system handles the catalogue, not that it is safe; the safety argument depends on how completely the functional scenarios were derived from the hazard analysis and operational design domain, which needs independent review.

Results are only as credible as the simulation. If the models of sensors, vehicle dynamics or other road users have not been validated against the real world, a system can pass in simulation and fail in operation, so key scenarios should be repeated on a test track or against recorded real data.

How concrete scenarios are sampled shapes what the results mean. Covering whole parameter ranges ignores how often each situation occurs, and searching for critical corner cases finds failures efficiently but over-represents rare situations, so neither supports a statement about real-world accident rates unless results are weighted by how often scenarios occur.

Pass criteria encode a judgement about acceptable behaviour. 'No collision' misses near misses and lucky escapes, while criticality measures such as time-to-collision need thresholds that the developer must choose and justify, and the verdicts change with them.

Building scenario catalogues, simulation environments and behaviour models for other road users takes specialist effort and substantial computing, and ISO 34502 covers automated driving on limited-access highways only, so other road types and other domains must adapt the framework themselves.

sample_claims.text: The motorway driving function passed every concrete scenario sampled from the cut-in, cut-out and stopped-vehicle logical scenarios derived from the hazard analysis, with no collisions and minimum time-to-collision above the agreed threshold.
In simulated reconstructions of the fatal crashes recorded in its operating area, the driving system avoided every crash in which it replaced the driver who initiated the conflict.
The ferry's collision-avoidance planner kept the required passing distance in every simulated head-on, crossing and overtaking encounter across the specified ranges of speed, bearing and visibility.
The scenario catalogue used for release testing covers every hazardous event identified in the hazard analysis and the full operational design domain, as confirmed by independent review.
